Croatia cuts hospital arrears

After years of mounting debts in the public health system, Croatia has started to clear the unpaid invoices that hospitals owed to their suppliers. The turnaround follows a structural reform supported by the European Commission through its technical support instrument, which helped the ministry of health redesign how hospitals plan budgets, procure medicines and report liabilities. Officials say the new approach gives managers clearer rules and earlier warnings when spending drifts away from the agreed envelope.

Hospital arrears fell by 40 percent between 2021 and 2023. Analysts attribute the decline mainly to centralised procurement, a monthly reporting duty for every public hospital, and a dedicated team that negotiates repayment schedules with suppliers. Pharmaceutical companies, which had complained for a decade about late payments of several hundred days, now report that average payment delays have shortened considerably and that contracts are being renewed on better terms for both sides.

The reform was not limited to financial controls. Experts from the Commission worked alongside Croatian civil servants to map the flow of money from the national insurance fund to individual hospitals, and to identify the services that were systematically underfunded. The resulting recommendations led to updated tariffs for several procedures, a clearer split between emergency and planned care, and a pilot programme that lets regional hospitals share expensive equipment rather than buying it separately.

Not everyone is fully convinced that the improvement will last. Hospital directors point out that wage increases agreed with unions are raising costs faster than revenues, and that an ageing population will push demand higher over the coming years. Independent economists argue that the progress on arrears should be monitored for several more years before it is called permanent, and they recommend publishing hospital level data every quarter so that citizens and journalists can follow developments.

For the Commission, the Croatian case is being presented as an example of how targeted technical support can produce measurable results in a short period. Other member states facing similar problems with public sector liabilities have asked to learn from the experience, and a series of workshops is planned for next year. Croatian officials say they are happy to share their tools, including the reporting templates, the procurement guidelines and the training material used by hospital finance teams.
